title: Stop selling covered calls after a crash and volatility spike
summary: After a crash, implied volatility is high and premiums look fat. The speaker does the opposite of most sellers: he stops selling covered calls and adds convexity in a vega-sensitive way. Every sold option caps your upside. He expects the rebound to pay more than the extra premium, so he does not cap the upside at the wrong time.

steps.caption: After a crash the stock trades at $80 and implied volatility jumps to about 55%.
Shares alone keep the full rebound. Every dollar of recovery above $80 is yours.
A covered call collects the fat premium but caps the gain at the $88 strike.
The difference is the upside you give away in a sharp rebound. It can be far more than the premium.
The premium only lowers the breakeven a little. It does not protect much if the fall continues.

takeaways: Every option you sell caps your upside: a covered call at the strike, a cash-secured put at the premium.
After a crash the rebound can pay more than the higher premium.
There are times to sell premium and times not to. Do not cap the upside at the wrong time.
caveats: Adding convexity after a crash is a view on a rebound, not a certainty. Strikes and prices are example values.
